title: The other handle
hookLine: everything has two handles; take your brother by "he is my brother," not "he wronged me" (Enchiridion 43)

cards: A pot on the stove has two handles. One has been sitting over the flame, and it's scorching. The other is cool.
Grab the hot one and you drop the pot, and now there's soup on the floor and a burn on your hand. Nobody would blame the pot. You just picked it up by the wrong side.
Section forty-three of the Enchiridion is about that choice, and Epictetus aims it straight at family.

teach.b: Everything has two handles, Epictetus says: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it can't. The pot is today's picture, not his, but the handles are his.

If your brother wrongs you, he says, don't take hold of it by the handle he wronged me. That's the handle by which it can't be carried. Take it by the other one: he's my brother, we were raised together.
Then you'll be holding it by the handle that can be carried. The wrong still happened; Epictetus doesn't pretend otherwise. What changes is which fact you pick up first.
Grab he wronged me, and every other fact arranges itself around the injury.
Grab he's my brother, and the injury becomes one fact inside a longer story, a story with a shared childhood and a kitchen table and probably a few wrongs going the other way.
Same situation, different handle, different weight. It works beyond brothers. A coworker, a neighbor, a parent, a friend who let you down.

teach.h: EVERY RELATIONSHIP HAS A COOL HANDLE.
teach.b: Each relationship has its own cool handle: she's been loyal for ten years. He's my father. We've built this together.
And a look back at the week, since today closes it: my own size. Mind the step.
The foot measures. Honor the character. Mind first.
It seemed right to him. Yesterday and today belong together: first you see why they did it, then you choose how to hold it.

how: People practicing Stoicism often reframe a conflict with someone close by starting from the relationship rather than the offense, following Epictetus' image of the two handles.

o: one side a thing can be carried by, and one it can't
two sides of an argument that are equally right
a pair of choices where both lead to the same end

games.q: the other handle — tap the pairs.
p: the handle that can't be carried
which fact you pick up first

s: Epictetus says to pretend the wrong never happened
the wrong is real; you choose which handle to lift it by.
the image of two handles comes from Enchiridion 43
one by which a thing can be carried, one by which it can't.
the hot pot on the stove is Epictetus' own example
the pot is today's picture; his example is the brother who wrongs you.

games.q: your brother has wronged you, again. you can feel the hot handle in your hand. what does Epictetus suggest?
o: hold it by he wronged me, so you don't forget.
take it by the other handle: he's my brother, we grew up together.
put it down and never speak to him.
games.why: take it by the handle that can be carried: he's your brother, raised with you. the wrong is still there, but it weighs differently.

practice: Bring to mind one conflict you're carrying with someone close, and notice which handle you've been holding it by: what they did, what they said, how hot it is.
Then gently look for the other handle: who they are to you, what you've shared, what's true about them besides this. Pick the whole thing up by that one fact, and notice the difference in weight.

wordCard.voice: Two handles, Epictetus says everything has: one that can be carried, and one that can't. Pick up your brother by the one that can. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a handle, a grip. Enchiridion 43 says everything has two.

carryVoice: Your line: he's my brother. The cool handle is often the older story. Day three hundred seventy-eight, and another week done.
